frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify Electron’x Professional Group investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current professional laundry offering.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Current reach to individual buyers is unknown and must be discovered.
Any recommendation must be based on evidence of demand, willingness to pay, or competitive advantage.
Financial and contractual details may not be public.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., home laundry, small businesses, or a new segment) with unique features and branding.
2) Expand the existing professional offering into adjacent consumer segments (e.g., add‑on accessories, subscription services, or a consumer‑focused brand) without a differentiated proposition.
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on the professional laundry and food‑service equipment business.
4) Partner with or license the professional technology to consumer brands rather than creating a direct consumer proposition.

T1.claim: Homeowners and small businesses increasingly adopt self‑service laundry solutions because they value convenience, cost savings, and reduced wait times, creating demand for consumer‑operated machines that are easy to use and maintain.
T1.who_benefits: Residents, guests, and members in multi‑family buildings, student housing, campsites, marinas, gyms, and staff facilities who need independent laundry access.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: These users currently rely on public laundromats or professional services; self‑service machines eliminate the need for scheduling, queue‑management, and external staff, making laundry more accessible and time‑efficient.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Electrolux can capture value by selling consumer‑grade machines at premium prices, leveraging its professional‑grade components and brand reputation to justify higher costs and by offering accessories, maintenance contracts, and service for
assumptions: Self‑service adoption is growing in residential and small‑business segments.
Consumers are willing to pay a premium for reliability and ease of use over cheaper alternatives.
Electrolux’s professional‑grade reputation can be leveraged to build trust in consumer products.
Distribution channels (e.g., retail, wholesale) can reach these segments effectively.
predictions: In a test offering a consumer‑grade self‑service unit to a sample of homeowners and small‑business tenants, at least 30% will express intent to purchase or lease within 12 weeks.
Surveyed users will rank convenience and cost savings as the top reasons for choosing a self‑service machine over public laundromats or professional services.
Sales conversion will be higher in regions with higher density of multi‑family buildings and student housing.
T1.first_claim: Homeowners and small businesses increasingly adopt self‑service laundry solutions because they value convenience, cost savings, and reduced wait times, creating demand for consumer‑operated machines that are easy to use and maintain.

T2.claim: Homeowners and small businesses adopt self‑service laundry solutions because they seek cost‑of‑ownership savings and lower long‑term maintenance expenses, making durable, professional‑grade machines an attractive financial choice.
T2.who_benefits: Residents, guests, and members in multi‑family buildings, student housing, campsites, marinas, gyms, and staff facilities who need independent laundry access and want to reduce recurring repair and replacement costs.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: These users currently pay for public laundromats or professional services, which incur ongoing fees and wear. Self‑service machines eliminate these recurring costs and offer a single, durable unit that lasts longer than domestic appliances.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Electrolux can capture value by selling consumer‑grade machines at premium prices justified by their professional‑grade components and longer expected lifespan, and by offering maintenance contracts and service that reduce long‑term costs.
assumptions: Consumers are price‑sensitive and prioritize total cost of ownership over brand reputation.
Professional‑grade durability translates into lower replacement and repair frequency for consumers.
Electrolux’s reputation for reliability can be leveraged to justify higher consumer prices.
Distribution channels can reach these segments effectively.
predictions: In a test offering a consumer‑grade self‑service unit to a sample of homeowners and small‑business tenants, at least 25% will indicate cost savings as the primary reason for choosing the machine.
Surveyed users will rank lower upfront cost and higher durability as the top factors influencing purchase decisions.
Sales conversion will be higher in regions with higher cost‑of‑ownership concerns for public laundromats or professional services.
T2.first_claim: Homeowners and small businesses adopt self‑service laundry solutions because they seek cost‑of‑ownership savings and lower long‑term maintenance expenses, making durable, professional‑grade machines an attractive financial choice.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify Electron’x Professional Group investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current professional laundry offering.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Current reach to individual buyers is unknown and must be discovered.
Any recommendation must be based on evidence of demand, willingness to pay, or competitive advantage.
Financial and contractual details may not be public.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., home laundry, small businesses, or a new segment) with unique features and branding.
2) Expand the existing professional offering into adjacent consumer segments (e.g., add‑on accessories, subscription services, or a consumer‑focused brand) without a differentiated proposition.
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on the professional laundry and food‑service equipment business.
4) Partner with or license the professional technology to consumer brands rather than creating a direct consumer proposition.

T1.claim: Homeowners will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition if they perceive it as a premium, safety‑and‑health product that reduces laundry effort and offers a premium experience.
T1.who_benefits: Homeowners seeking convenience, safety, and a premium laundry experience.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: They currently rely on traditional laundry methods or low‑end machines, and a differentiated proposition that emphasizes professional‑grade safety, convenience, and design would shift their purchase decision from necessity to choice.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Electrolux can charge a premium price for a differentiated line, sell through specialty retailers or direct channels, and capture margin on higher‑priced units.
assumptions: Homeowners are willing to pay a premium for perceived safety and convenience.
Electrolux can differentiate its products with unique features such as advanced safety certifications, smart connectivity, and design.
Retail or direct channels can effectively reach and convert this segment.
predictions: A survey of homeowners would show higher intent to purchase a differentiated consumer line compared to a standard professional line.
Sales of the differentiated line would be higher in regions where laundry effort is a significant pain point.
Willingness to pay would be above the price of comparable consumer machines.
T1.first_claim: Homeowners will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition if they perceive it as a premium, safety‑and‑health product that reduces laundry effort and offers a premium experience.

T2.claim: Homeowners will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition if it offers a subscription or service model that reduces ongoing maintenance and provides convenience, because they value low effort and predictable costs.
T2.who_benefits: Homeowners who want a hassle‑free laundry solution with no upfront cost.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: They currently pay for a machine and ongoing repairs, and a subscription or service model removes that burden, making ownership more attractive.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Electrolux can monetize through recurring subscription fees or service contracts, capturing recurring revenue and higher margins than a one‑time purchase.
assumptions: Homeowners are willing to pay a recurring fee for convenience.
A subscription or service model can be delivered at scale without significant additional cost.
Regulatory or service constraints do not prevent this model.
predictions: A pilot offering a subscription would show higher retention and repeat purchase rates than a standard purchase.
Willingness to pay would be lower for a subscription compared to a one‑time purchase, but overall revenue would be higher.
Customers would report lower perceived effort and higher satisfaction with the subscription model.

position.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. Public evidence shows residential customers are demanding commercial‑quality home appliances and that Electron‑x already sells consumer‑operated units, but it does not demonstrate that homeowners will pay a premium or that they need high‑capacity units. Conduct the proposed Consumer vs Multi‑Family Messaging Test to measure purchase intent before committing.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify Electron’x Professional Group investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current professional laundry offering.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Current reach to individual buyers is unknown and must be discovered.
Any recommendation must be based on evidence of demand, willingness to pay, or competitive advantage.
Financial and contractual details may not be public.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., home laundry, small businesses, or a new segment) with unique features and branding.
2) Expand the existing professional offering into adjacent consumer segments (e.g., add‑on accessories, subscription services, or a consumer‑focused brand) without a differentiated proposition.
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on the professional laundry and food‑service equipment business.
4) Partner with or license the professional technology to consumer brands rather than creating a direct consumer proposition.

T1.claim: Homeowners and small businesses will adopt professional-grade laundry equipment if they perceive it as a premium, long‑life product that reduces their own laundry effort and costs.
T1.who_benefits: Homeowners and small business owners who currently do laundry themselves and seek convenience and cost savings.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: They will switch from doing laundry at home to using a professional machine because they view it as a professional-grade, long‑term investment that saves time and money compared to domestic appliances.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Electrolux can capture value by pricing the consumer offering at a premium (e.g., 20‑30% above domestic models) and selling through retail channels, leveraging its professional reputation to command higher prices.
assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay a premium for professional‑grade reliability and durability.
The perception of professional quality influences purchase decisions.
Retail distribution is feasible without disrupting the professional business.
predictions: In a test offering a consumer‑grade machine at a 25% premium over a comparable domestic model, at least 15% of surveyed homeowners will express intent to purchase within 12 weeks.
Sales conversion rate will be higher in a retail setting than online, indicating demand for physical interaction.
T1.first_claim: Homeowners and small businesses will adopt professional-grade laundry equipment if they perceive it as a premium, long‑life product that reduces their own laundry effort and costs.

T2.claim: Homeowners and small businesses will adopt professional-grade laundry equipment if they need a reliable, high‑capacity solution for multi‑family buildings, student housing, or commercial spaces where domestic appliances are insufficient.
T2.who_benefits: Multi‑family property owners, property managers, and small business owners who require a durable, high‑volume washing and drying unit.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: They will switch from domestic appliances to professional machines because they need a unit that can handle multiple loads daily, reduces downtime, and provides consistent performance for a large number of users.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Electrolux can capture value by offering high‑capacity models with extended warranties and service contracts, and by selling through wholesale channels to property managers and rental companies.
assumptions: High‑volume demand exists in multi‑family and commercial settings.
Consumers are willing to invest in a professional machine for operational reliability.
Wholesale distribution can reach these segments effectively.
predictions: In a test offering a high‑capacity consumer machine to property managers, at least 20% will express intent to purchase within 12 weeks.
Sales conversion will be higher when presented as a rental or lease option rather than a direct purchase.

X1.name: Consumer vs Multi‑Family Messaging Test
X1.method: Online survey with randomized messaging. Participants are recruited from homeowners and small business owners. Half see a consumer‑grade machine described as a premium, long‑life home appliance (T1). The other half see a high‑capacity machine described as a reliable, high‑volume solution for multi‑family buildings (T2). Both see identical product specifications and pricing (e.g., 25% premium over domestic models). Participants indicate purchase intent on a 7‑point scale and whether they would purchase now or in 12 weeks.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify Aquaporin A/S investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current water-membrane offering.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeframe for any proposed experiment.
Current reach to individual buyers is unknown; must be discovered.
Any recommendation must be based on evidence of demand, willingness to pay, or competitive advantage.
Investment decision must be justified by clear evidence of consumer need, market opportunity, or competitive differentiation.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., home water purifier for a niche segment).
2) Expand the existing water‑membrane offering to new markets or customer segments without a differentiated proposition (e.g., B2B expansion).
3) No expansion: continue focusing on current B2B membranes and existing distribution channels.
4) Partner with or license the technology to consumer brands rather than selling under Aquaporin A/S brand.
5) Pursue a subscription or service model for membrane maintenance or performance monitoring.

T1.claim: Consumers will adopt a differentiated home water purifier if they perceive it as a premium, convenience product that reduces maintenance and offers a clear safety benefit, leading to higher purchase intent and willingness to pay.
T1.who_benefits: Aquaporin A/S would benefit by capturing premium pricing and building brand equity in the consumer market.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: If consumers shift from viewing water purifiers as a necessary utility to a lifestyle or convenience product, they will be willing to pay more for a product that requires less maintenance and provides a measurable safety benefit.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Aquaporin can capture value by selling differentiated units at premium prices, leveraging its biomimetic membrane technology as a differentiator, and potentially through subscription or service models for maintenance.
assumptions: Consumers currently perceive water purifiers as a utility rather than a lifestyle product.
A premium positioning can be communicated effectively to the target segment.
The maintenance burden is a significant pain point for current consumers.
predictions: In a test offering a differentiated premium purifier, purchase intent among target consumers will be at least 20% higher than for a standard membrane unit.
Willingness to pay for the premium unit will be at least 15% above the price of a standard unit.
Surveyed consumers will cite reduced maintenance as the primary reason for choosing the premium product.
T1.first_claim: Consumers will adopt a differentiated home water purifier if they perceive it as a premium, convenience product that reduces maintenance and offers a clear safety benefit, leading to higher purchase intent and willingness to pay.

T2.why_behaviour_changes: If consumers view water quality as a critical health and environmental issue, they will be willing to invest in a product that delivers superior water quality, even at a higher cost.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Aquaporin can capture value by pricing the product at a premium, emphasizing health and environmental benefits, and potentially through partnerships with health and sustainability-focused brands.

Willingness to pay for the health-environment positioned unit will be at least 15% above the price of a standard unit.
Surveyed consumers will cite water quality improvement as the primary reason for choosing the health-environment product.

position.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that positions the water purifier as a health-necessity premium product, leveraging Aquaporin's proprietary membrane technology to communicate safety and peace-of-mind benefits. This approach aligns with evidence of consumer perception of tap water as unhealthy and the willingness to pay a premium for branded, high-performance products.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify Aquaporin A/S investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current water-membrane offering.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeframe for any proposed experiment.
Current reach to individual buyers is unknown; must be discovered.
Any recommendation must be based on evidence of demand, willingness to pay, or competitive advantage.
Investment decision must be justified by clear evidence of consumer need, market opportunity, or competitive differentiation.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., home water purifier for a niche segment).
2) Expand the existing water‑membrane offering to new markets or customer segments without a differentiated proposition (e.g., B2B expansion).
3) No expansion: continue focusing on current B2B membranes and existing distribution channels.
4) Partner with or license the technology to consumer brands rather than selling under Aquaporin A/S brand.
5) Pursue a subscription or service model for membrane maintenance or performance monitoring.

X1.name: Willingness-to-Pay Survey for Differentiated Consumer Water Purifier
X1.method: Online survey with randomized messaging and willingness-to-pay (WTP) questions.
X1.sample: 500 Danish homeowners (ages 25-55) recruited via an online panel, stratified by household income and water purity concerns.
X1.measure: Average WTP in euros for a branded water purifier marketed as either (a) a health necessity premium product or (b) a convenience/cost-saving subscription service.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Higher average WTP for the health-necessity premium product (price above €200) than for the convenience subscription.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Higher average WTP for the convenience subscription service than for the health-necessity premium product.

X1.decision_rule: If the average WTP for the health-necessity premium product exceeds the average WTP for the convenience subscription by at least €50, proceed with developing a differentiated consumer proposition focused on health necessity. If the opposite difference holds, proceed with a convenience-focused proposition. If the difference is within €50, conduct a follow-up survey to resolve ambiguity.

revisions.reason: The simulated maintenance-convenience proposition test (SYN-AQP-UPDATE) does not address consumer perception of health necessity or willingness to pay a premium for a differentiated consumer proposition. It tests willingness to enroll in a maintenance offer under a conditional supply assumption, which does not change the dossier evidence about Aquaporin's insolvency or financing. Therefore, the theory remains intact.

arguments.name: Willingness-to-Pay Survey for Differentiated Consumer Water Purifier
arguments.method: Online survey with randomized messaging and willingness-to-pay (WTP) questions.
arguments.sample: 500 Danish homeowners (ages 25-55) recruited via an online panel, stratified by household income and water purity concerns.
arguments.measure: Average WTP in euros for a branded water purifier marketed as either (a) a health necessity premium product or (b) a convenience/cost-saving subscription service.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Higher average WTP for the health-necessity premium product (price above €200) than for the convenience subscription.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Higher average WTP for the convenience subscription service than for the health-necessity premium product.

arguments.decision_rule: If the average WTP for the health-necessity premium product exceeds the average WTP for the convenience subscription by at least €50, proceed with developing a differentiated consumer proposition focused on health necessity. If the opposite difference holds, proceed with a convenience-focused proposition. If the difference is within €50, conduct a follow-up survey to resolve ambiguity.

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

arguments.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that positions the water purifier as a health-necessity premium product, leveraging Aquaporin's proprietary membrane technology to communicate safety and peace-of-mind benefits. This approach aligns with evidence of consumer perception of tap water as unhealthy and the willingness to pay a premium for branded, high-performance products.

result.title: Simulated maintenance-convenience proposition test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. Treat the following only as a what-if. In this hypothetical randomized study, 800 households already using a compatible drinking-water purifier received the same membrane specifications, water-quality information, brand, warranty and total annual price. Half were offered a prepaid plan with scheduled cartridge delivery and replacement reminders; half were offered a prepaid self-service cartridge plan without that delivery schedule or reminders. There were no discounts. The outcome was a paid plan enrollment remaining uncancelled after 30 days, counted among all 400 assigned households per arm. This what-if assumes an authorised operator can legally supply and service the offer; it does not change the dossier evidence about Aquaporin's insolvency or financing. There were 60 plan enrollments in the scheduled-delivery-and-reminder plan arm and 120 in the self-service cartridge plan arm. This tests willingness to enroll in a maintenance offer under that conditional supply assumption, not membrane efficacy, correct long-term filter use, market size, company solvency or Aquaporin's ability to fund an offer. An unchanged business recommendation can be justified by those other constraints.
result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

arguments.reason: The simulated maintenance-convenience proposition test (SYN-AQP-UPDATE) does not address consumer perception of health necessity or willingness to pay a premium for a differentiated consumer proposition. It tests willingness to enroll in a maintenance offer under a conditional supply assumption, which does not change the dossier evidence about Aquaporin's insolvency or financing. Therefore, the theory remains intact.

tool_result.title: Simulated maintenance-convenience proposition test
tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. Treat the following only as a what-if. In this hypothetical randomized study, 800 households already using a compatible drinking-water purifier received the same membrane specifications, water-quality information, brand, warranty and total annual price. Half were offered a prepaid plan with scheduled cartridge delivery and replacement reminders; half were offered a prepaid self-service cartridge plan without that delivery schedule or reminders. There were no discounts. The outcome was a paid plan enrollment remaining uncancelled after 30 days, counted among all 400 assigned households per arm. This what-if assumes an authorised operator can legally supply and service the offer; it does not change the dossier evidence about Aquaporin's insolvency or financing. There were 60 plan enrollments in the scheduled-delivery-and-reminder plan arm and 120 in the self-service cartridge plan arm. This tests willingness to enroll in a maintenance offer under that conditional supply assumption, not membrane efficacy, correct long-term filter use, market size, company solvency or Aquaporin's ability to fund an offer. An unchanged business recommendation can be justified by those other constraints.
tool_result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify Aquaporin A/S investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current water-membrane offering.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.

Current reach to individual buyers is unknown; must be discovered.
Any recommendation must be based on evidence of demand, willingness to pay, or competitive advantage.
Investment decision must be justified by clear evidence of consumer need, market opportunity, or competitive differentiation.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., home water purifier for a niche segment).

In this hypothetical randomized study, 800 households already using a compatible drinking-water purifier received the same membrane specifications, water-quality information, brand, warranty and total annual price. Half were offered a prepaid plan with scheduled cartridge delivery and replacement reminders; half were offered a prepaid self-service cartridge plan without that delivery schedule or reminders. There were no discounts. The outcome was a paid plan enrollment remaining uncancelled after 30 days, counted among all 400 assigned households per arm. This what-if assumes an authorised operator can legally supply and service the offer; it does not change the dossier evidence about Aquaporin's insolvency or financing. There were 60 plan enrollments in the scheduled-delivery-and-reminder plan arm and 120 in the self-service cartridge plan arm. This tests willingness to enroll in a maintenance offer under that conditional supply assumption, not membrane efficacy, correct long-term filter use, market size, company solvency or Aquaporin's ability to fund an offer. An unchanged business recommendation can be justified by those other constraints.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify Aquaporin A/S investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current water-membrane offering.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeframe for any proposed experiment.
Current reach to individual buyers is unknown; must be discovered.
Any recommendation must be based on evidence of demand, willingness to pay, or competitive advantage.
Investment decision must be justified by clear evidence of consumer need, market opportunity, or competitive differentiation.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., home water purifier for a niche segment).
2) Expand the existing water‑membrane offering to new markets or customer segments without a differentiated proposition (e.g., B2B expansion).
3) No expansion: continue focusing on current B2B membranes and existing distribution channels.
4) Partner with or license the technology to consumer brands rather than selling under Aquaporin A/S brand.
5) Pursue a subscription or service model for membrane maintenance or performance monitoring.

T1.claim: Home water purifier owners treat their devices as a medical necessity and will pay a premium for a membrane that delivers high water quality, so a manufacturer that controls membrane design and brand can capture value by selling premium-priced units.
T1.who_benefits: Homeowners with high water quality needs (e.g., those with hard water, lead, or chemical contamination concerns).
T1.why_behaviour_changes: They perceive water quality as a health and safety issue and are willing to pay more for a membrane that consistently delivers superior performance.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Aquaporin can charge a premium price for its membrane and brand, and potentially through subscription or service models for maintenance.
assumptions: Consumers are aware of water quality issues and are willing to invest in solutions.
The membrane's performance is demonstrably superior to competitors.
There is a large enough segment of homeowners willing to pay a premium.
predictions: In a test offering a differentiated premium-priced purifier, purchase intent or actual purchases will be higher than for a standard-priced unit.
Surveyed buyers will cite water quality as the primary reason for choosing the product.
T1.first_claim: Home water purifier owners treat their devices as a medical necessity and will pay a premium for a membrane that delivers high water quality, so a manufacturer that controls membrane design and brand can capture value by selling premium-priced units.

T2.claim: Homeowners treat water purifiers as a convenience and a status symbol, so they will purchase multiple units or upgrade frequently, creating recurring revenue for a manufacturer that can offer a subscription or service model.
T2.who_benefits: Homeowners who value convenience, status, and ongoing service rather than a single purchase.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: They view the purifier as an essential household item and are willing to pay for maintenance, monitoring, and replacement services.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Aquaporin can capture value through subscription fees, service contracts, and data-driven performance monitoring.
assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay for ongoing maintenance and monitoring.
The subscription or service model is cost-effective for both parties.
There is a segment of homeowners who frequently upgrade or purchase multiple units.
predictions: In a test offering a subscription or service model, repeat purchase or upgrade rates will be higher than for a one-time purchase.
Surveyed buyers will cite convenience and status as primary reasons for choosing the subscription.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify Aquaporin A/S investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current water-membrane offering.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.

alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., home water purifier for a niche segment).

X1.name: Positioning Test: Health vs Convenience Messaging
X1.method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants are recruited from a panel of health-conscious and convenience-focused consumers. Each participant sees one of two product descriptions for the same Aquaporin water purifier: Health-focused (emphasizing water quality improvement, reduced contaminants, and premium positioning). The other description is a convenience-focused version (emphasizing easy installation, low maintenance, and smart home integration). After viewing the description, participants indicate purchase intent (1‑10 scale) and maximum price they would pay.
X1.sample: 300 participants (150 per condition) from a panel of Danish consumers aged 25–45, balanced for health and convenience preferences.
X1.measure: Purchase intent score (1‑10) and maximum price willingness to pay for each condition.

X1.decision_rule: If the average purchase intent for the health-focused condition is at least 5 points higher than the convenience-focused condition, proceed with a health‑focused differentiated proposition. If the difference is less than 5 points, proceed with a convenience‑focused differentiated proposition. If the difference is less than 2 points, do not expand; consider other alternatives.

arguments.name: Positioning Test: Health vs Convenience Messaging
arguments.method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants are recruited from a panel of health-conscious and convenience-focused consumers. Each participant sees one of two product descriptions for the same Aquaporin water purifier: Health-focused (emphasizing water quality improvement, reduced contaminants, and premium positioning). The other description is a convenience-focused version (emphasizing easy installation, low maintenance, and smart home integration). After viewing the description, participants indicate purchase intent (1‑10 scale) and maximum price they would pay.
arguments.sample: 300 participants (150 per condition) from a panel of Danish consumers aged 25–45, balanced for health and convenience preferences.
arguments.measure: Purchase intent score (1‑10) and maximum price willingness to pay for each condition.

prediction_by_theory.T2: Convenience-focused condition will generate higher purchase intent and higher willingness to pay than health-focused condition.

result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. Treat the following only as a what-if. In this hypothetical randomized study, 800 households already using a compatible drinking-water purifier received the same membrane specifications, water-quality information, brand, warranty and total annual price. Half were offered a prepaid plan with scheduled cartridge delivery and replacement reminders; half were offered a prepaid self-service cartridge plan without that delivery schedule or reminders. There were no discounts. The outcome was a paid plan enrollment remaining uncancelled after 30 days, counted among all 400 assigned households per arm. This what-if assumes an authorised operator can legally supply and service the offer; it does not change the dossier evidence about Aquaporin's insolvency or financing. There were 120 plan enrollments in the scheduled-delivery-and-reminder plan arm and 60 in the self-service cartridge plan arm. This tests willingness to enroll in a maintenance offer under that conditional supply assumption, not membrane efficacy, correct long-term filter use, market size, company solvency or Aquaporin's ability to fund an offer. An unchanged business recommendation can be justified by those other constraints.

tool_result.title: Simulated maintenance-convenience proposition test
tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. Treat the following only as a what-if. In this hypothetical randomized study, 800 households already using a compatible drinking-water purifier received the same membrane specifications, water-quality information, brand, warranty and total annual price. Half were offered a prepaid plan with scheduled cartridge delivery and replacement reminders; half were offered a prepaid self-service cartridge plan without that delivery schedule or reminders. There were no discounts. The outcome was a paid plan enrollment remaining uncancelled after 30 days, counted among all 400 assigned households per arm. This what-if assumes an authorised operator can legally supply and service the offer; it does not change the dossier evidence about Aquaporin's insolvency or financing. There were 120 plan enrollments in the scheduled-delivery-and-reminder plan arm and 60 in the self-service cartridge plan arm. This tests willingness to enroll in a maintenance offer under that conditional supply assumption, not membrane efficacy, correct long-term filter use, market size, company solvency or Aquaporin's ability to fund an offer. An unchanged business recommendation can be justified by those other constraints.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify Aquaporin A/S investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current water-membrane offering.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.

alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., home water purifier for a niche segment).

T1.claim: Home water purifier owners treat membranes as a durable, low‑maintenance component. If they perceive a membrane as a one‑time purchase, they will not pay a premium for a differentiated consumer proposition, so a manufacturer that offers a differentiated proposition must justify a premium by demonstrating superior durability or longer replacement intervals.

T1.why_behaviour_changes: Owners currently replace membranes every 6‑12 months; a differentiated proposition promising longer replacement intervals or superior performance would shift purchase decisions from frequency to performance.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Value is captured through premium pricing for a differentiated product and through recurring revenue from replacement membranes or service contracts.
assumptions: Current replacement frequency is 6‑12 months for most membranes.
Performance differences between membrane types are measurable and communicateable to consumers.

X1.name: Membrane Durability vs TCO Choice Test
X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase decision. Participants view two membrane options (standard vs differentiated) and are asked to indicate willingness to pay (WTP) and purchase intent. The differentiated option is described with a longer replacement claim (T1) or a TCO savings claim (T2). Randomization ensures each participant sees only one option.
X1.sample: 300 adult homeowners with existing water purifiers, recruited via an online panel to match demographic distribution of the target market.
X1.measure: WTP (in euros) and purchase intent (1‑10 scale). Secondary measure: stated importance of replacement frequency vs TCO savings.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Higher WTP and purchase intent for the differentiated option when the claim is about longer replacement intervals.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Higher WTP and purchase intent for the differentiated option when the claim is about TCO savings (lower replacement frequency or reduced operational costs).

X1.decision_rule: If the differentiated option's WTP is at least 20% higher than the standard option, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition. If the difference is less than 20% or the TCO claim does not significantly outperform the durability claim, do not invest in a differentiated proposition. If both claims perform equally, conduct further market research.

frame.objective: Determine whether Simonelli Group should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current professional espresso-equipment offering, based on evidence of market demand, competitive positioning, and feasibility within budget and time constraints.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.

Current reach to individual buyers is unknown and must be discovered.
Any recommendation must be justified by evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, and Simonelli’s ability to capture value.
Any expansion must consider Simonelli’s existing professional brand and its ability to differentiate without cannibalizing the professional segment.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., home barista, small office, travel) with a new product or marketing approach.

assumptions: Status-driven consumers are a significant segment of the home coffee market.
Simonelli can effectively communicate status positioning to these consumers.
The current professional brand does not cannibalize the consumer proposition.
predictions: When a home machine is marketed as a status item, purchase intent among high-income consumers increases relative to a functional positioning.
Sales of the status-positioned home machine will be higher than sales of a similar machine marketed purely as a functional product.

Simonelli’s existing professional reputation transfers to consumer positioning.

predictions: When a home machine is marketed on reliability and consistent performance, purchase intent among consumers increases relative to a machine marketed on status.

X1.name: Status vs Reliability Messaging Test
X1.method: Online survey with simulated product descriptions. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two messaging conditions: (A) status positioning (e.g., 'Oscar Mood is the Italian manufacturer’s first step towards a new frontier and a status item for home coffee enthusiasts.') or (B) reliability positioning (e.g., 'Oscar Mood is equipped with PID technology and ensures professional-quality coffee at home, delivering consistent results every time.')
X1.sample: 300 adult consumers interested in home coffee equipment, recruited via an online panel, balanced for income and self-reported purchase intent.
X1.measure: Purchase intent measured on a 7-point Likert scale (1 = very unlikely, 7 = very likely) and willingness to pay a premium price (EUR).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Higher purchase intent and willingness to pay in the status condition than in the reliability condition.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Higher purchase intent and willingness to pay in the reliability condition than in the status condition.

X1.decision_rule: If the mean purchase intent in the status condition exceeds the mean in the reliability condition by at least 1.5 points on the 7-point scale, we conclude that status-driven demand is more likely and recommend developing a status-positioned consumer proposition. If the reliability condition exceeds the status condition by at least 1.5 points, we conclude reliability-driven demand is more likely and recommend a reliability-positioned proposition. If the difference is <1.5 points, we conclude neither mechanism dominates and recommend further research.

revisions.reason: The simulated result (SYN-SIMO-UPDATE) tests a learning proposition (home-barista lesson) among home espresso enthusiasts, not status-driven demand. It does not address T1, which predicts status-driven purchase behavior. Therefore T1 remains unchanged.

position.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that positions Simonelli home machines as visible status items, targeting high-income consumers who value conspicuous consumption. Use marketing that emphasizes elegance, professional quality, and social signaling to capture premium pricing and margins.

frame.objective: Determine whether Simonelli Group should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current professional espresso-equipment offering, based on evidence of market demand, competitive positioning, and feasibility within budget and time constraints.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Current reach to individual buyers is unknown and must be discovered.
Any recommendation must be justified by evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, and Simonelli’s ability to capture value.
Any expansion must consider Simonelli’s existing professional brand and its ability to differentiate without cannibalizing the professional segment.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., home barista, small office, travel) with a new product or marketing approach.
2) Expand the existing professional line into adjacent consumer segments (e.g., add consumer-friendly accessories, co‑brands, or a subscription service) without a new differentiated proposition.
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on the professional espresso-equipment business and not pursue consumer propositions.
4) Partner with or license Simonelli’s technology to third‑party consumer brands rather than selling under Simonelli’s own consumer brand.

There were 32 reservations in the home-barista-lesson offer arm and 72 in the product-specification-orientation offer arm. frame.objective: Determine whether Simonelli Group should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current professional espresso-equipment offering, based on evidence of market demand, competitive positioning, and feasibility within budget and time constraints.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.

Current reach to individual buyers is unknown and must be discovered.
Any recommendation must be justified by evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, and Simonelli’s ability to capture value.
Any expansion must consider Simonelli’s existing professional brand and its ability to differentiate without cannibalizing the professional segment.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., home barista, small office, travel) with a new product or marketing approach.
2) Expand the existing professional line into adjacent consumer segments (e.g., add consumer-friendly accessories, co‑brands, or a subscription service) without a new differentiated proposition.
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on the professional espresso-equipment business and not pursue consumer propositions.
4) Partner with or license Simonelli’s technology to third‑party consumer brands rather than selling under Simonelli’s own consumer brand.

X1.name: Status vs Reliability Messaging Test
X1.method: Online survey with randomized messaging conditions. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups: Status Group (home machine marketed as a visible status item) or Reliability Group (home machine marketed on consistent performance). Both groups see a description of the same Simonelli home machine.
X1.sample: 400 adult consumers interested in home coffee equipment, recruited via an online panel. Randomly split into 200 per condition.
X1.measure: Purchase intent measured on a 7-point scale (1 = very unlikely, 7 = very likely) and willingness to pay (EUR). Secondary measure: stated importance of status vs reliability.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Status Group will show higher purchase intent and willingness to pay than Reliability Group.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Reliability Group will show higher purchase intent and willingness to pay than Status Group.

X1.decision_rule: If the difference in average purchase intent between Status and Reliability Groups is at least 1.5 points on the 7-point scale, and the Status Group's average is at least 1.5 points higher, then T1 is supported. If the Reliability Group's average is at least 1.5 points higher, then T2 is supported. If the difference is less than 1.5 points or neither group is significantly higher, the test is inconclusive and no expansion is recommended.

result.excerpt: We conduct an experiment in which we vary both whether a purchase of a physical product is publicly visible or kept private and whether the income used for purchase is linked to social status or randomly assigned. Making consumption choices visible leads to a large increase in demand when income is linked to status, but not otherwise.

arguments.why_behaviour_changes: Consumers with higher income and status values are more likely to publicly display purchases of visible goods, leading to increased demand when the purchase is framed as a status statement.

predictions: When a home machine is marketed as a status item, purchase intent among high-income consumers increases relative to a functional positioning.

arguments.name: Status vs Reliability Messaging Test
arguments.method: Online survey with randomized messaging conditions. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups: Status Group (home machine marketed as a visible status item) or Reliability Group (home machine marketed on consistent performance). Both groups see a description of the same Simonelli home machine.
arguments.sample: 400 adult consumers interested in home coffee equipment, recruited via an online panel. Randomly split into 200 per condition.
arguments.measure: Purchase intent measured on a 7-point scale (1 = very unlikely, 7 = very likely) and willingness to pay (EUR). Secondary measure: stated importance of status vs reliability.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Status Group will show higher purchase intent and willingness to pay than Reliability Group.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Reliability Group will show higher purchase intent and willingness to pay than Status Group.

arguments.decision_rule: If the difference in average purchase intent between Status and Reliability Groups is at least 1.5 points on the 7-point scale, and the Status Group's average is at least 1.5 points higher, then T1 is supported. If the Reliability Group's average is at least 1.5 points higher, then T2 is supported. If the difference is less than 1.5 points or neither group is significantly higher, the test is inconclusive and no expansion is recommended.

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

arguments.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. The evidence shows Simonelli already offers a home-focused machine (Linea Micra) and has a consumer line (Oscar Mood), but it does not demonstrate that status-driven consumers will purchase it or that the existing professional brand will cannibalize the consumer segment. A limited test is needed to measure purchase intent under status versus reliability fram

result.title: Simulated home-barista learning proposition test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. Treat the following only as a what-if. In this hypothetical randomized study, 800 home espresso enthusiasts considering the same Simonelli single-group machine were assigned equally to two offers. Machine, brand, price, warranty, availability and total contact time were identical. One offer included a structured hands-on home-barista setup lesson; the other included an equal-length product-specification orientation without a skill lesson. There were no discounts. The outcome was a paid, refundable machine reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days, counted among all 400 assigned enthusiasts per arm. There were 72 reservations in the home-barista-lesson offer arm and 32 in the product-specification-orientation offer arm. This tests the incremental effect of this learning offer among recruited enthusiasts, not a need for a new machine, demand among ordinary coffee drinkers, commercial margins or lasting skill retention. It does not show that every hobby or status mechanism is true or false.

position.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that positions Simonelli home machines as visible status items, targeting high-income consumers who value social signaling. This approach leverages existing brand prestige and aligns with evidence that conspicuous consumption drives demand when income is linked to status.

frame.objective: Determine whether Simonelli Group should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current professional espresso-equipment offering, based on evidence of market demand, competitive positioning, and feasibility within budget and time constraints.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Current reach to individual buyers is unknown and must be discovered.
Any recommendation must be justified by evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, and Simonelli’s ability to capture value.
Any expansion must consider Simonelli’s existing professional brand and its ability to differentiate without cannibalizing the professional segment.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., home barista, small office, travel) with a new product or marketing approach.
2) Expand the existing professional line into adjacent consumer segments (e.g., add consumer-friendly accessories, co‑brands, or a subscription service) without a new differentiated proposition.
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on the professional espresso-equipment business and not pursue consumer propositions.
4) Partner with or license Simonelli’s technology to third‑party consumer brands rather than selling under Simonelli’s own consumer brand.

result.title: Simulated home-barista learning proposition test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. Treat the following only as a what-if. In this hypothetical randomized study, 800 home espresso enthusiasts considering the same Simonelli single-group machine were assigned equally to two offers. Machine, brand, price, warranty, availability and total contact time were identical. One offer included a structured hands-on home-barista setup lesson; the other included an equal-length product-specification orientation without a skill lesson. There were no discounts. The outcome was a paid, refundable machine reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days, counted among all 400 assigned enthusiasts per arm. There were 72 reservations in the home-barista-lesson offer arm and 32 in the product-specification-orientation offer arm. This tests the incremental effect of this learning offer among recruited enthusiasts, not a need for a new machine, demand among ordinary coffee drinkers, commercial margins or lasting skill retention. It does not show that every hobby or status mechanism is true or false.

tool_result.title: Simulated home-barista learning proposition test
tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. Treat the following only as a what-if. In this hypothetical randomized study, 800 home espresso enthusiasts considering the same Simonelli single-group machine were assigned equally to two offers. Machine, brand, price, warranty, availability and total contact time were identical. One offer included a structured hands-on home-barista setup lesson; the other included an equal-length product-specification orientation without a skill lesson. There were no discounts. The outcome was a paid, refundable machine reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days, counted among all 400 assigned enthusiasts per arm. There were 72 reservations in the home-barista-lesson offer arm and 32 in the product-specification-orientation offer arm. This tests the incremental effect of this learning offer among recruited enthusiasts, not a need for a new machine, demand among ordinary coffee drinkers, commercial margins or lasting skill retention. It does not show that every hobby or status mechanism is true or false.

position.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. The evidence shows Simonelli already offers a home-focused machine (Oscar Mood) and a compact home machine (Linea Micra), but it does not prove that status-driven consumers will purchase them. A limited test is needed to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay under status versus reliability messaging.

frame.objective: Determine whether Simonelli Group should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current professional espresso-equipment offering, based on evidence of market demand, competitive positioning, and feasibility within budget and time constraints.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Current reach to individual buyers is unknown and must be discovered.
Any recommendation must be justified by evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, and Simonelli’s ability to capture value.
Any expansion must consider Simonelli’s existing professional brand and its ability to differentiate without cannibalizing the professional segment.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., home barista, small office, travel) with a new product or marketing approach.
2) Expand the existing professional line into adjacent consumer segments (e.g., add consumer-friendly accessories, co‑brands, or a subscription service) without a new differentiated proposition.
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on the professional espresso-equipment business and not pursue consumer propositions.
4) Partner with or license Simonelli’s technology to third‑party consumer brands rather than selling under Simonelli’s own consumer brand.

X1.name: Status vs Reliability Messaging Test
X1.method: Online choice-based conjoint survey with simulated purchase. Participants view two home machine descriptions (Status vs Reliability positioning) and a price point. They indicate purchase intent (1‑10) and maximum willingness to pay (WTP).
X1.sample: 300 adult home coffee consumers recruited via an online panel, balanced for income and prior coffee equipment ownership.
X1.measure: Purchase intent (binary) and average WTP (in euros) for each positioning.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Status positioning yields higher purchase intent and higher WTP than reliability positioning.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Reliability positioning yields higher purchase intent and higher WTP than status positioning.

X1.decision_rule: If purchase intent for status positioning is at least 15 percentage points higher than for reliability positioning AND the difference in WTP is at least €50, proceed to develop a status‑focused consumer proposition. If reliability‑positioning intent is at least 15 percentage points higher AND the WTP difference is at least €50, develop a reliability‑focused proposition. If neither difference meets the thresholds, do not expand into consumer propositions.

revisions.reason: The simulated result (SYN-SIMO-UPDATE) tests a learning proposition (home-barista lesson) among home espresso enthusiasts, not a status mechanism. It does not address whether status drives purchase decisions, so it does not affect T1.

position.recommendation: Develop a differentiated home-cook proposition built on RATIONAL’s combi-steamer technology, leveraging its premium positioning and health benefits to capture discretionary home-cook demand.

frame.objective: Determine whether RATIONAL AG should develop a differentiated proposition for home cooks using its commercial combi-steamer technology, or remain focused on professional kitchens, based on evidence of market demand, competitive positioning, and feasibility within budget and time constraints.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Current reach to individual buyers is unknown; must be discovered.
Any recommendation must be justified by evidence of demand, willingness to pay, or competitive advantage.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated home‑cook proposition (e.g., a consumer‑grade combi‑steamer with unique features, branding, and distribution).
2) Stay focused on professional kitchens only (no new consumer offering).
3) Expand into adjacent consumer segments (e.g., small‑kitchen appliances) without altering the core combi‑steamer technology.

result.title: Simulated installation-coordination offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home cooks considering the same professional-derived combi-steamer were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed identical equipment, brand, cooking specifications, total installed price, warranty, available delivery dates and eventual plumbing/electrical work. One offer bundled an installation coordinator and a site-readiness checklist; the other required the purchaser to arrange the same qualified installers directly. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. All recruited homes were eligible for the stated installation work. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned households per arm. There were 72 reservations for the coordinated-installation offer and 32 for the purchaser-arranged offer. This tests whether coordination friction changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that the appliance fits ordinary kitchens, eliminates drain or power requirements, earns a margin, or justifies diverting resources from professional customers. It does not establish market size or a need for new RATIONAL hardware. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow coordination mechanism changes.

tool_result.title: Simulated installation-coordination offer test
tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home cooks considering the same professional-derived combi-steamer were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed identical equipment, brand, cooking specifications, total installed price, warranty, available delivery dates and eventual plumbing/electrical work. One offer bundled an installation coordinator and a site-readiness checklist; the other required the purchaser to arrange the same qualified installers directly. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. All recruited homes were eligible for the stated installation work. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned households per arm. There were 72 reservations for the coordinated-installation offer and 32 for the purchaser-arranged offer. This tests whether coordination friction changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that the appliance fits ordinary kitchens, eliminates drain or power requirements, earns a margin, or justifies diverting resources from professional customers. It does not establish market size or a need for new RATIONAL hardware. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow coordination mechanism changes.

result.title: Simulated installation-coordination offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home cooks considering the same professional-derived combi-steamer were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed identical equipment, brand, cooking specifications, total installed price, warranty, available delivery dates and eventual plumbing/electrical work. One offer bundled an installation coordinator and a site-readiness checklist; the other required the purchaser to arrange the same qualified installers directly. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. All recruited homes were eligible for the stated installation work. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned households per arm. There were 32 reservations for the coordinated-installation offer and 72 for the purchaser-arranged offer. This tests whether coordination friction changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that the appliance fits ordinary kitchens, eliminates drain or power requirements, earns a margin, or justifies diverting resources from professional customers. It does not establish market size or a need for new RATIONAL hardware. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow coordination mechanism changes.

tool_result.title: Simulated installation-coordination offer test
tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home cooks considering the same professional-derived combi-steamer were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed identical equipment, brand, cooking specifications, total installed price, warranty, available delivery dates and eventual plumbing/electrical work. One offer bundled an installation coordinator and a site-readiness checklist; the other required the purchaser to arrange the same qualified installers directly. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. All recruited homes were eligible for the stated installation work. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned households per arm. There were 32 reservations for the coordinated-installation offer and 72 for the purchaser-arranged offer. This tests whether coordination friction changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that the appliance fits ordinary kitchens, eliminates drain or power requirements, earns a margin, or justifies diverting resources from professional customers. It does not establish market size or a need for new RATIONAL hardware. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow coordination mechanism changes.

alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated home‑cook proposition (e.g., a consumer‑grade combi‑steamer with unique features, branding, and distribution).

4) No expansion: maintain current product portfolio and market focus.

X1.name: Design vs. Time-Saving Messaging Test
X1.method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants are recruited from home cooks who have purchased a kitchen appliance in the past year. They are randomly assigned to one of two message conditions: Design Condition (premium aesthetics, modern look, kitchen styling) or Time-Saving Condition (time savings, faster cooking, reduced prep time). Both conditions include a detailed product description of a RATIONAL combi-steamer. Participants indicate willingness to pay (WTP) and purchase intent on a 7-point scale.
X1.sample: 300 home cooks (150 per condition) recruited via an online panel to ensure representation across age, gender, and cooking frequency.
X1.measure: Willingness to pay (WTP) and purchase intent on a 7-point scale for each condition.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Design Condition will show higher WTP and purchase intent than Time-Saving Condition.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Time-Saving Condition will show higher WTP and purchase intent than Design Condition.

X1.decision_rule: If the average WTP for Design Condition is at least 20 points higher than for Time-Saving Condition (i.e., Design Condition average ≥ 5.5), recommend developing a differentiated home-cook proposition focused on design and aesthetics. If Time-Saving Condition average is at least 20 points higher, recommend a time-saving proposition. If neither difference meets the threshold, recommend no expansion.

result.title: Simulated installation-coordination offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home cooks considering the same professional-derived combi-steamer were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed identical equipment, brand, cooking specifications, total installed price, warranty, available delivery dates and eventual plumbing/electrical work. One offer bundled an installation coordinator and a site-readiness checklist; the other required the purchaser to arrange the same qualified installers directly. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. All recruited homes were eligible for the stated installation work. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned households per arm. There were 32 reservations for the coordinated-installation offer and 72 for the purchaser-arranged offer. This tests whether coordination friction changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that the appliance fits ordinary kitchens, eliminates drain or power requirements, earns a margin, or justifies diverting resources from professional customers. It does not establish market size or a need for new RATIONAL hardware. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow coordination mechanism changes.

arguments.name: Smart vs Premium Home Cook Messaging Test
arguments.method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants are recruited from a panel of home cooks (frequency of cooking at home). arguments.measure: Willingness to pay (WTP) and purchase intent (1‑2 scale) for the premium professional‑grade (T1) versus the smart‑connected (T2) messaging.

prediction_by_theory.T2: Higher WTP and purchase intent for the smart‑connected messaging than for the premium professional‑grade messaging.

arguments.decision_rule: If the average WTP for premium professional‑grade messaging exceeds the average WTP for smart‑connected messaging by at least 15 percentage points, recommend developing a differentiated home‑cook proposition (T1). If the difference is less than 15 percentage points, recommend staying focused on professional kitchens (no new consumer offering). If the difference is not detectable, recommend no expansion.

result.title: Simulated installation-coordination offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home cooks considering the same professional-derived combi-steamer were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed identical equipment, brand, cooking specifications, total installed price, warranty, available delivery dates and eventual plumbing/electrical work. One offer bundled an installation coordinator and a site-readiness checklist; the other required the purchaser to arrange the same qualified installers directly. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. All recruited homes were eligible for the stated installation work. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned households per arm. There were 32 reservations for the coordinated-installation offer and 72 for the purchaser-arranged offer. This tests whether coordination friction changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that the appliance fits ordinary kitchens, eliminates drain or power requirements, earns a margin, or justifies diverting resources from professional customers. It does not establish market size or a need for new RATIONAL hardware. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow coordination mechanism changes.
result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

arguments.reason: The simulated installation-coordination offer test (SYN-RATIONAL-UPDATE) does not address home-cook demand for premium professional-grade combi-steamers. It tests a narrow coordination mechanism and does not establish market size, price sensitivity, or willingness to pay for a consumer model. Therefore it does not affect T1.
